title: Reading p
summary: What a p-value does and doesn't say, how confidence intervals and p agree, and how to report both in APA style.
hints: p is calculated assuming H₀ is true, so it can't be the probability that H₀ is true.
With a big enough sample, any nonzero difference becomes significant.
APA: italic p, no leading zero, exact values down to .001.

quiz.prompt: A study reports p = .03. Which statement is correct?
choices: There's a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true
There's a 97% chance the effect is real
If H₀ were true, results at least this extreme would turn up about 3% of the time
The effect is small
quiz.explain: p is computed *assuming* H₀ is true, so it can't also be the probability that H₀ is true. It's the probability of data at least this extreme under H₀, the share you counted in the Courtroom's retrial.

quiz.prompt: Study A (n = 20 per group) finds p = .04; study B (n = 2,000 per group) finds p = .0001. Which found the bigger effect?
choices: Study B, because its p is smaller
Study A, because it reached significance with fewer people
You can't tell from p: it mixes effect size with sample size. Compare the effect sizes
They found the same effect
quiz.explain: A tiny effect with a huge sample gives a tiny p, as you saw in the Courtroom. p answers "is it surprising under H₀?", not "is it big?". That's why APA asks for an effect size (such as Cohen's d) alongside every test.

quiz.prompt: A 95% CI for a difference in means is [−0.8, 4.2]. What does a two-sided test at α = .05 conclude?
choices: Significant, because most of the interval is positive
Not significant, because the interval includes 0
Significant, because the interval excludes 4.2
You can't tell without the p-value
quiz.explain: A 95% CI and a two-sided test at α = .05 always agree: the test rejects H₀ (difference = 0) exactly when 0 lies outside the interval. Here 0 is inside, so p > .05. The CI says more, though: it shows which differences are plausible, from slightly negative to quite large.
Italic *p*, no leading zero (p can't exceed 1), usually three decimals. A value that rounds to .000 is reported as *p* < .001, never p = .000.

quiz.prompt: p = .07 with α = .05. How should it be written up?
choices: "The difference approached significance"
"There was a trend towards a difference"
"The difference was not statistically significant, p = .07", with the effect size and CI
Leave the result out of the paper
quiz.explain: Results are either below α or not; "approaching significance" treats .07 as nearly .05 only when it's convenient. Report the exact p, the effect size and its CI, and let the reader judge. Leaving out non-significant results biases the literature.

quiz.prompt: A colleague runs 20 different tests on their data, finds one with p = .04 and reports only that one. What's the problem?
choices: Nothing, p = .04 is below .05
With 20 tests and no real effects, about one false alarm at α = .05 is expected
They should have used α = .01 for that one test only
They should report p = .040
quiz.explain: α = .05 is the false-alarm rate *per test*. Run 20 and the chance of at least one false alarm is about 64%. Reporting only the hit is a form of p-hacking. Pre-register the tests you plan, report all of them, and correct for multiple comparisons when needed (you'll meet Bonferroni and Tukey in the Variance Rift).
